Safe home

Heat and cold

How to protect your pet from overheating and hypothermia.

Contents
  1. 1. Summer heat
  2. 2. Heatstroke risk!
  3. 3. Winter
  4. 4. Hidden dangers
  5. 5. Something to keep in mind
1

Summer heat

  • Always keep a bowl of fresh water within reach. Cats drink more when they're hot.
  • Use cooling mats or damp towels, but don't force your cat to lie on them.
  • Avoid direct drafts from the air conditioner — ideally, the cool air should not blow directly on the cat. Clean the AC filters as needed.

Don't:

  • don't pour ice water on your cat;
  • don't apply ice directly to its body;
  • don't force it to drink.
2

Heatstroke risk!

Caution

Watch for:

  • rapid open-mouthed breathing;
  • severe lethargy;
  • bright red gums;
  • refusal to eat or drink;
  • loss of coordination.

If these symptoms appear, urgent veterinary care may be needed.

3

Winter

Cozy beds off the floor, plus humidifying dry indoor air. Create warm spots around the house: bedding and a draft-free location will help retain warmth.

In winter it's important to:

  • avoid drafts;
  • not place the bed near a cold window;
  • maintain 40–60% humidity;
  • and wipe your cat's paws after walks (if it goes outside).
4

Hidden dangers

Hot radiators — prolonged contact can cause burns. Tilted-open windows — a risk of hypothermia and injury.

5

Something to keep in mind

Tip

Cats choose their own comfortable temperature. If your pet keeps lying on the cold floor, hiding under a blanket, or staying by the radiator, that's a sign it's too hot or too cold for it.
